title: The Economics of Socially Legitimate Energy Transitions: Testing Smart Energy Policies Employing Synthetic Economic Agents
content: Energy policies that appear cost-efficient in engineering models may be economically infeasible when households decline to participate, distrust institutions, or anticipate unfair bills and loss of privacy. This paper presents Acceptability-Constrained Smart Energy Design (ACSED), a socio-technical framework in which social legitimacy is an endogenous constraint on the design of distributed energy systems. ACSED combines calibrated large language models as cultural world models, heterogeneous synthetic economic agents, social interaction, and energy-system simulation to test policy packages before implementation. Its economic contribution is to bring adoption frictions, perceived risks, distributional impacts, transaction costs, and institutional arrangements inside the comparison of smart meters, dynamic tariffs, rooftop photovoltaics, batteries, electric-vehicle charging, heat pumps, and energy communities. This research suggests that governance provisions such as privacy protection, bill-risk safeguards, and local participation can change the feasible policy set, even where they add direct costs. Synthetic agents are a policy-screening instrument rather than substitutes for surveys or democratic consent. ACSED offers a research agenda for assessing technically effective policies against their real prospects of legitimate economic implementation.
